questions.question:
A satellite is moved from a low Earth orbit (LEO) to a geostationary orbit (GEO), as shown in the diagram.

The satellite will now be able to:
options: image the surface of the entire Earth.
take more detailed images of the Earth.
continuously monitor the same location on Earth.
move over the surface of the Earth and therefore scan a larger area of the Earth.
questions.answer: A geostationary satellite orbits above the equator with a period of 24 hours, the same as Earth's rotation, so it stays above the same point on the surface and can monitor that location continuously. (Being much further away, it takes *less* detailed images, and it cannot see the whole Earth.)

questions.question:
An experimental setup designed to measure the speed of light is shown below (a light source, a rotating toothed cogwheel and a mirror 8 km away).

Which statement best describes the experiment?
options: A historical method of measuring the speed of light using distance and time.
A contemporary method of measuring the speed of light using distance and time.
A historical method of measuring the speed of light using frequency and wavelength.
A contemporary method of measuring the speed of light using frequency and wavelength.
questions.answer: This is Fizeau's rotating toothed-wheel experiment (1849), a historical method. The light travels a known distance ($2 \times 8$ km) and the time taken is found from the rotation rate of the wheel that just blocks the returning light, so $c = \dfrac{d}{t}$.

questions.question:
The diagram below shows a key experiment in the development of the atomic model: alpha particles from a source are fired at a thin gold foil.

Which statement correctly identifies the development, and the scientist who proposed the development of the model?
options: De Broglie — that electrons could behave as waves.
questions.answer: This is the Geiger–Marsden gold-foil experiment. The small number of alpha particles deflected through large angles led Rutherford to propose that the atom's positive charge and most of its mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.

questions.question:
Two points, 1 and 2, are labelled on a rotating disk as shown below. Point 1 is closer to the centre than point 2.

What is the relationship between the linear speed ($v$) and angular speed ($\omega$) at points 1 and 2?
questions.answer: All points on a rigid rotating disk sweep out the same angle in the same time, so $\omega_1 = \omega_2$. Since $v = \omega r$ and $r_1 < r_2$, $v_1 < v_2$.

questions.question:
The following graph shows the radiation emitted from a black body at a range of wavelengths.

How would the peak intensity and wavelength of maximum intensity of the curve change if the black body temperature was increased?
options: Both peak intensity and wavelength of maximum intensity would increase.
Both peak intensity and wavelength of maximum intensity would decrease.
Peak intensity would increase, wavelength of maximum intensity would decrease.
Peak intensity would decrease, wavelength of maximum intensity would increase.
questions.answer: A hotter black body emits more radiation at every wavelength, so the peak intensity increases. By Wien's law $\lambda_{\max} = \dfrac{b}{T}$, so the wavelength of maximum intensity decreases.

questions.question:
The following Hertzsprung–Russell diagram shows stars at various stages in their life cycle (labelled L, M, N, O and P).

Which of the following is a possible evolutionary sequence for a star?
questions.answer: M is a main sequence star (similar to the Sun), O is a red giant (cool, luminous) and L is a white dwarf (hot, very dim). A Sun-like star evolves from the main sequence to a red giant and finishes as a white dwarf: M $\rightarrow$ O $\rightarrow$ L.

questions.question:
An AC generator is operated so that the coil has a constant rotational speed. The output voltage is shown on the graph below (peak 2 V, two complete cycles in 0.1 s).

The rotation speed of the coil is halved. Which of the following graphs represents the new output voltage?
questions.answer: Halving the rotation speed halves the frequency (so only one cycle occurs in 0.1 s) and, since $\varepsilon = -N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$, the rate of change of flux is halved, so the peak emf halves from 2 V to 1 V. Graph D shows both.

questions.question:
A proton moving parallel to a constant electric field is accelerating at $1.15 \times 10^{6}\ \text{km s}^{-2}$.

What is the strength of the electric field?
questions.answer:
$F = ma$ and $F = qE$, so
$$E = \frac{ma}{q} = \frac{1.673 \times 10^{-27} \times 1.15 \times 10^{9}}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 12\ \text{N C}^{-1}.$$
(Note: $1.15 \times 10^6$ km s$^{-2}$ $= 1.15 \times 10^9$ m s$^{-2}$. The paper printed the unit as km s$^{-1}$, a typo for an acceleration.)

questions.question:
The spectra of three stars, X, Y and Z, moving away from the Earth are shown (wavelength increases from 400 nm on the left to 700 nm on the right).

What is the correct ranking of the THREE stars' density ($D$) and translational velocity ($v$)?
questions.answer: Recession velocity is shown by red shift: Z's lines are shifted furthest towards longer wavelengths, then Y, then X, so $v_z > v_y > v_x$. Density (pressure) is shown by line broadening: X has the broadest lines, then Z, and Y the narrowest, so $D_x > D_z > D_y$.

questions.question:
A laser was shone onto a double slit which produced an interference pattern on a screen as shown in the diagram, with slit separation $d$, slit-to-screen distance $L$ and bright-band spacing $\Delta x$.

What changes to the slit separation ($d$) and distance to screen ($L$) will both increase the distance between two bright bands ($\Delta x$)?
questions.answer: For small angles $\Delta x = \dfrac{\lambda L}{d}$, so the fringe spacing increases when $d$ is decreased and when $L$ is increased.

questions.question:
An astronaut is on a spacecraft travelling at $0.85c$ past a football field. The astronaut measures the length of the football field as 63.4 m.

What is the length of the football field as measured on Earth?
questions.answer:
The field is at rest on Earth, so Earth measures the proper length $l_0$; the astronaut measures the contracted length $l$.
$$l = l_0\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}} \;\Rightarrow\; l_0 = \frac{63.4}{\sqrt{1 - 0.85^2}} = \frac{63.4}{0.5268} \approx 120\ \text{m}.$$

questions.question:
The diagrams below show part of the electricity distribution network (power plant, transformer 1, transmission lines, transformer 2, distribution lines, 3 = entering house, 4 = 12 V appliances) and a transformer that is found in at least one location within the network. The transformer has more turns on its primary winding than on its secondary winding.

Where in the distribution network would this transformer be located, and what is its purpose in this location?
options: 2 – used to step down voltage to the Australian household standard of 240 V.
1 – used to step up voltage so energy is not lost in long distance transmission wires.
2 and 3 – used to step down voltage to allow high voltage appliances to be used in households.
3 and 4 – used to step down voltage so it can be used safely in a range of household appliances.
questions.answer: The transformer has more primary than secondary turns, so it is a step-down transformer ($\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s} > 1$). Step-down transformers near the house (3) reduce the distribution voltage to 240 V, and at the appliance (4) reduce 240 V to 12 V, so the voltage can be used safely. Location 1 needs a step-up transformer, and location 2 steps down only to the distribution voltage, not to 240 V.

questions.question:
A solenoid connected to an ammeter (terminals X and Y) is lowered onto a magnet that is fixed to a table, with the magnet's north pole facing up, as shown.

What is the direction of current through the coil, and the direction of the magnetic force on the solenoid as it moves downwards?
options: Current X to Y; force upwards
Current X to Y; force downwards
Current Y to X; force upwards
Current Y to X; force downwards
questions.answer: As the solenoid approaches the north pole, the flux through it increases. By Lenz's law the induced current opposes this change, so the bottom of the solenoid becomes a north pole that repels the magnet — the magnetic force on the solenoid is upwards (opposing its motion). Applying the right-hand grip rule to the windings shown, a north pole at the bottom requires the current to flow through the coil from X to Y.

questions.question:
Alpha, beta and gamma radiation is passed through a magnetic field directed into the page. The resulting paths are shown below: K curves upwards slightly, L travels in a straight line and M curves sharply downwards.

Rank the three types of radiation in order of increasing ionising and penetrating power.
options: Ionising power: L, M, K; penetrating power: K, M, L
Ionising power: K, M, L; penetrating power: L, M, K
Ionising power: K, L, M; penetrating power: K, M, L
Ionising power: L, M, K; penetrating power: K, L, M
questions.answer: L is undeflected, so it is gamma (uncharged). With $\mathbf{B}$ into the page and motion to the right, $F = qvB$ pushes positive charges up, so K is alpha (positive, heavy, so only slightly curved) and M is beta (negative, light, strongly curved). Ionising power increases gamma < beta < alpha (L, M, K); penetrating power increases alpha < beta < gamma (K, M, L).

questions.question:
The following graph shows how the magnetic flux $\Phi_B$ through a coil changes over time.

What is the approximate emf generated in this coil between 0.02 and 0.04 s?
questions.answer:
Between 0.02 s and 0.04 s the flux changes from $-0.03$ Wb to $+0.03$ Wb.
$$\varepsilon = -\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = -\frac{0.03 - (-0.03)}{0.02} = -3\ \text{V}.$$

questions.question:
An object attached to a rod is moving in a vertical circle at a constant speed. P is the top of the circle and Q is the bottom.

The magnitudes of the forces involved with the motion of the object include tension ($F_T$), gravitational ($F_g$) and centripetal ($F_C$) forces.

What is the magnitude of the net force acting on the object at P and Q?
options: At P: $F_T - F_g$; at Q: $F_T - F_g$
At P: $F_T + F_g$; at Q: $F_T - F_g$
At P: $F_T + F_g$; at Q: $F_T + F_g$
questions.answer: At P (top) both the tension and the weight act downwards, towards the centre, so the net force is $F_T + F_g$. At Q (bottom) the tension acts upwards (towards the centre) and the weight downwards, so the net force is $F_T - F_g$. In both cases this net force provides the centripetal force.

questions.question:
Three polarisation filters F1, F2 and F3 are set up in a line as shown below. F1 is oriented vertically, at 0°. Unpolarised light is passed into F1.

What combination of angles from the vertical for F2 and F3 would result in light leaving F3 at 30% of the initial intensity?
questions.answer:
F1 transmits half of the unpolarised light, so 50% leaves F1. We need $\dfrac{30}{50} = \cos^2\theta_{12}\cos^2\theta_{23}$.

B: F2 at 180° is parallel to F1 ($\cos^2 180° = 1$) and F3 is $39°$ from F2: $0.5 \times 1 \times \cos^2 39° = 0.5 \times 0.604 = 0.30$, i.e. 30%. ✔

Check others: A gives $0.5\cos^2 20°\cos^2 39° \approx 27\%$; C gives $0.5\cos^2 57° \approx 15\%$; D gives $0.5\cos^2 45°\cos^2 6° \approx 25\%$.

questions.question:
A radioactive isotope is known to have one measurable emission for each decay a nucleus in the sample undergoes.

A sample of the isotope was measured to have 148 962 126 emissions in 6 hours and 15 minutes. At the start of the measurement time, the sample had $1.642 \times 10^{9}$ nuclei present.

Calculate the approximate half-life of the radioactive isotope.
questions.answer:
$N_t = 1.642 \times 10^9 - 148\,962\,126 = 1.4930 \times 10^9$ and $t = 6 \times 3600 + 15 \times 60 = 22\,500$ s.
$$N_t = N_0 e^{-\lambda t} \Rightarrow \lambda = \frac{1}{22\,500}\ln\!\left(\frac{1.642 \times 10^9}{1.4930 \times 10^9}\right) = 4.23 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{s}^{-1}$$
$$t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda} \approx 1.6 \times 10^{5}\ \text{s}.$$

questions.question:
A student used a diffraction grating to split the visible wavelengths emitted by hydrogen gas in a discharge tube. The student observed coloured lines at points L, M, N and O, at increasing angles from the central line (L closest to the centre, O furthest). [The diagram is not drawn to scale.]

Which statement correctly describes the spectral transition lines observed from hydrogen gas?
options: M corresponds to a transition starting at $n = 5$.
O corresponds to a transition that started at the $n = 7$ energy level.
L corresponds to the highest energy level transition possible in hydrogen.
The electron that produced O transitioned down more energy levels than the electron that produced L.
questions.answer: The visible hydrogen lines are the Balmer series (transitions to $n = 2$). From $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$, a smaller angle means a shorter wavelength. The four visible lines are 410 nm ($6 \to 2$), 434 nm ($5 \to 2$), 486 nm ($4 \to 2$) and 656 nm ($3 \to 2$), so L is $6 \to 2$, M is $5 \to 2$, N is $4 \to 2$ and O is $3 \to 2$. Hence M starts at $n = 5$. (O drops fewer levels than L, and L is not the highest possible transition.)

questions.question:
Two satellites orbit the same planet. Satellite A has a period that is 8 times smaller than satellite B.

Calculate the ratio of the speeds $v_A : v_B$ of the two satellites.
questions.answer:
By Kepler's third law $r^3 \propto T^2$. With $T_B = 8T_A$: $r_B^3 = 64 r_A^3$, so $r_B = 4r_A$.

Orbital speed $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$, so
$$\frac{v_A}{v_B} = \frac{r_A}{r_B}\cdot\frac{T_B}{T_A} = \frac{1}{4} \times 8 = 2.$$
Hence $v_A : v_B = 2 : 1$.

questions.question:
A single coil ABCD carrying a current from a battery is rotating in a magnetic field between the poles of a magnet, as shown below.

Identify TWO ways that the maximum torque on the coil in the diagram could be increased.

A green laser of wavelength 532 nm illuminates a double slit. The slits are 100 μm apart. The position of the central bright band on the screen is labelled P$_0$. The first two bright bands to one side are labelled P$_1$ and P$_2$.

Calculate the angle between P$_0$ and P$_2$ from the double slit.
questions.answer:
P$_2$ is the second-order maximum, so $m = 2$, with $\lambda = 532 \times 10^{-9}$ m and $d = 100 \times 10^{-6}$ m.
$$d\sin\theta = m\lambda \Rightarrow \sin\theta = \frac{2 \times 532 \times 10^{-9}}{100 \times 10^{-6}} = 0.01064$$
$$\theta = \sin^{-1}(0.01064) = 0.610^\circ\ \text{(3 s.f.)}$$

questions.question: Outline Maxwell's contributions to electromagnetic theory.
questions.answer:
- **Unification of electricity and magnetism:** Maxwell combined the work of Gauss, Faraday and Ampère into a single set of equations (Maxwell's equations), showing that a changing electric field produces a magnetic field and a changing magnetic field produces an electric field.
- **Prediction of electromagnetic waves:** from these equations he predicted that accelerating (oscillating) charges produce self-propagating waves of mutually perpendicular, oscillating electric and magnetic fields, and that such waves could exist over a whole range of frequencies/wavelengths beyond visible light (later confirmed by Hertz with radio waves).
- **Speed of light:** he calculated the speed of these waves as $c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}} \approx 3 \times 10^8$ m s$^{-1}$, equal to the measured speed of light, and so concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave.

questions.question:
An experiment is set up with two parallel copper rods, A and B, each of length 0.75 m, as shown below. Rod A is 2.0 mm above Rod B. Rod A is fixed in place and unable to move. Rod B is resting on an electronic balance and is free to move.

The electronic balance is zeroed so it reads 0 g with Rod B resting on the balance. No current is flowing through either rod.

A current of 5.6 A is now passed through both rods, with the current flowing in opposite directions in the two rods.

Determine the mass shown on the electronic balance, in grams, when the current is flowing through both rods.
questions.answer:
Force between the rods:
$$F = \frac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\frac{I_1 I_2}{r}\,l = \frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7}}{2\pi} \times \frac{5.6 \times 5.6}{2.0 \times 10^{-3}} \times 0.75 = 2.352 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{N}.$$
Currents in opposite directions repel, so rod B is pushed **downwards** onto the balance with an extra $2.352 \times 10^{-3}$ N. The balance (zeroed with B on it) interprets this as an extra mass:
$$\Delta m = \frac{F}{g} = \frac{2.352 \times 10^{-3}}{9.8} = 2.4 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{kg} = 0.24\ \text{g}.$$
The balance reads $0.24$ g.

questions.question:
In developing his theory of the expanding universe, Hubble collected spectra for various galaxies that were at known distances from Earth.

Explain how Hubble's analysis of spectra showed evidence for the expanding universe theory.
questions.answer:
- Hubble compared the absorption lines in the spectra of light from distant galaxies with the positions of the same lines (e.g. of hydrogen) measured in the laboratory on Earth.
- He found that the lines in the light from almost all galaxies were shifted towards longer wavelengths — the light was **red-shifted**.
- By the Doppler effect, light from a source moving away from the observer is stretched to longer wavelengths, so the red shift showed that these galaxies are receding from Earth; the size of the shift gives the recession velocity.
- Plotting recession velocity against the known distances showed a linear relationship ($v = H_0 d$): the further away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away.
- Galaxies moving away from us (and from each other) at speeds proportional to their distance is exactly what is expected if space itself is expanding and stretching the light, so his analysis provided evidence that the universe is expanding.

questions.question: Outline ONE similarity and ONE difference between the motion of a satellite in orbit, and a charged particle moving perpendicular to a magnetic field.
questions.answer:
**Similarity:** both undergo uniform circular motion, because each experiences a net (centripetal) force of constant magnitude that is always perpendicular to its velocity and directed towards the centre of the circle, so it changes the direction but not the speed: $F_c = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$.

**Difference:** for the satellite the centripetal force is provided by the gravitational attraction to the central body, $F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$, which depends on mass; for the charged particle the centripetal force is provided by the magnetic force $F = qvB$, which depends on its charge and speed and is perpendicular to both $v$ and $B$ (direction from the right-hand palm rule).

questions.question:
The photoelectric effect has a number of observable properties that cannot be explained by classical physics theory.

Analyse how the concept of a cut-off frequency of light in the photoelectric effect applies to both the wave and particle models of light.
questions.answer:
- **Cut-off (threshold) frequency:** for a given metal, no photoelectrons are emitted if the frequency of the incident light is below a certain value $f_0$, no matter how intense the light is or how long it shines; above $f_0$ emission is immediate.
- **Wave model:** classically, the energy of a wave depends on its amplitude (intensity), not its frequency, and is delivered continuously. Light of any frequency should therefore eventually give electrons enough energy to escape, given sufficient intensity or time. The wave model predicts no cut-off frequency, so it cannot explain the observation.
- **Particle (photon) model:** Einstein proposed that light consists of photons of energy $E = hf$, and that each photon transfers all its energy to a single electron (a one-to-one interaction). An electron is only emitted if $hf \geq \phi$, the work function of the metal, so there is a threshold frequency $f_0 = \dfrac{\phi}{h}$. Below $f_0$ no single photon has enough energy, and increasing the intensity only increases the number of photons, not their energy.
- Hence the cut-off frequency is explained only by the particle model ($K_{\max} = hf - \phi$), and it is key evidence against the wave model in this situation.

questions.question:
In an experiment using the photoelectric effect apparatus, the stopping voltage for photoelectrons emitted was measured.

Justify how the stopping voltage of the emitted photoelectrons would change if the intensity of the incoming light was doubled.
questions.answer:
The stopping voltage would **not change**.

- The stopping voltage $V_s$ is the reverse potential that just stops the most energetic photoelectrons reaching the collector, so $qV_s = K_{\max}$.
- By Einstein's photoelectric equation $K_{\max} = hf - \phi$, the maximum kinetic energy depends only on the photon frequency and the work function of the metal.
- Doubling the intensity (at the same frequency) doubles the number of photons striking the metal each second, and since each photon ejects at most one electron, it doubles the number of photoelectrons (the photocurrent), but each photon still has the same energy $hf$.
- So $K_{\max}$, and therefore the stopping voltage, stays the same.

questions.question:
A single square loop of conducting wire was moved through a uniform magnetic field (directed out of the page) at constant speed, as shown below: A — entering the field, B — completely within the field, C — exiting the field.

Analyse how the magnitude and direction of the current will change as the loop passes from outside the magnetic field on the left side (A), within the field (B), and passing out of the field on the right side (C).
questions.answer:
By Faraday's law, an emf is induced when the flux through the loop changes: $\varepsilon = -N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$, with $\Phi = BA_\perp$. As the loop is a complete circuit, the emf drives a current $I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R}$. Lenz's law gives the direction: the induced current creates a field that opposes the change in flux.

**A (entering):** the area of the loop inside the field increases at a constant rate, so the out-of-page flux increases at a constant rate, giving a constant emf and a constant current. To oppose the increase in out-of-page flux, the induced current produces a field into the page inside the loop, so the current flows **clockwise**.

**B (within the field):** the whole loop is in the uniform field, so the flux through it is constant: $\Delta\Phi = 0$, so there is no emf and **no current**.

**C (exiting):** the area inside the field decreases at the same constant rate, so the flux decreases at the same rate and the current has the **same magnitude** as at A. To oppose the decrease in out-of-page flux, the induced current produces a field out of the page inside the loop, so it flows **anticlockwise** — the opposite direction to A.

questions.question:
An object is launched vertically from the Earth's surface. After launch, the object has no engine or fuel providing any further force of propulsion.

The line on the graph below represents the gravitational potential energy of the object at a range of heights above the Earth's surface (negative, rising towards zero).

Sketch, on a copy of the graph, the line representing the kinetic energy of the object for the same range of heights.
questions.answer:
With no propulsion, mechanical energy is conserved: $U + K = \text{constant}$. So the kinetic energy curve must decrease with height by exactly as much as the potential energy increases — it is a mirror image of the $U$ curve, shifted so that $U + K$ is constant.

- If the object is launched at exactly escape velocity, $U + K = 0$, so $K = -U$: the $K$ curve is the reflection of the $U$ curve in the zero line, starting high and decreasing towards zero (left graph).
- If the total energy is less than zero (object does not escape), the $K$ curve is the same shape but shifted down, reaching zero at the maximum height (right graph).

Either is correct, provided $K$ decreases with height so that $U + K$ stays constant.

questions.question: Derive the equation for escape velocity, $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{r}}$, and thus show the escape velocity of Earth is 11.2 km s$^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
Escape velocity is the minimum launch speed for an object to just reach an infinite distance, where $U = 0$, with zero kinetic energy. So at escape velocity the total energy is zero, and since energy is conserved:
$$E_T = K + U = 0 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{GMm}{r} = 0 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{GMm}{r}$$
$$v^2 = \frac{2GM}{r} \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}}.$$
For Earth, with $M = 6.0 \times 10^{24}$ kg, $r = 6.371 \times 10^{6}$ m, $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ N m$^2$ kg$^{-2}$:
$$v = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6.0 \times 10^{24}}{6.371 \times 10^{6}}} = 11\,208\ \text{m s}^{-1} \approx 11.2\ \text{km s}^{-1}.$$

questions.question:
Nuclear fission, shown below, is used in nuclear power reactors to generate electricity. A neutron (1.008665 u) is absorbed by uranium-235 (235.0493 u), producing krypton-92 (91.8973 u), barium-141 (140.9139 u) and three neutrons (total 3.026 u).

Nuclear fusion occurs in stars and provides the heat and light energy produced by stars. A diagram of part of this process (a proton and a neutron fusing to form deuterium) is shown below.

The binding energy per nucleon graph below is related to both fission and fusion processes (it peaks at iron-56).

Analyse, qualitatively and quantitatively, the processes that occur in fission and fusion to release energy in nuclear reactors and stars.
questions.answer:
**Binding energy and mass defect.** Both fission and fusion release energy because the products have a smaller total mass than the reactants; the mass defect $\Delta m$ is converted to energy, $E = \Delta mc^2$. As the binding energy graph shows, binding energy per nucleon is greatest near iron-56. Nuclei heavier than iron (e.g. U-235, about 7.6 MeV/nucleon) can split into medium-sized nuclei (Kr-92, Ba-141, about 8.5 MeV/nucleon) that are more tightly bound, and nuclei lighter than iron (e.g. hydrogen) can fuse into heavier, more tightly bound nuclei. In both cases the increase in total binding energy is released, mostly as kinetic energy of the products and gamma radiation.

**Fission — quantitative.**
$${}^{1}_{0}\text{n} + {}^{235}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow {}^{92}_{36}\text{Kr} + {}^{141}_{56}\text{Ba} + 3\,{}^{1}_{0}\text{n}$$
Mass of reactants $= 1.008665 + 235.0493 = 236.057965$ u; mass of products $= 91.8973 + 140.9139 + 3.026 = 235.8372$ u.
$$\Delta m = 0.220765\ \text{u} \Rightarrow E = 0.220765 \times 931.5 \approx 206\ \text{MeV} \;(\approx 3.3 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{J})\ \text{per fission}.$$

**Fission in nuclear reactors.** A slow (thermal) neutron is absorbed by U-235, forming an unstable nucleus that splits, releasing about 206 MeV and 2–3 neutrons. These neutrons can cause further fissions — a chain reaction. A moderator (e.g. water or graphite) slows the fast neutrons by collisions so they are more likely to be captured by U-235. Control rods (e.g. boron or cadmium) absorb neutrons and are raised or lowered so that on average one neutron from each fission causes another fission, keeping the chain reaction controlled (not exponential as in a bomb). The kinetic energy of the fragments heats the coolant, producing steam that drives turbines and generators to make electricity.

**Fusion in stars.** Fusion joins light nuclei (e.g. the proton and neutron forming deuterium in the diagram) into a heavier, more tightly bound nucleus, releasing the mass defect as energy. Because nuclei are positively charged, very high core temperatures and pressures (about $10^7$ K) are needed for nuclei to overcome Coulomb repulsion and come close enough for the strong nuclear force to act. Main sequence stars fuse hydrogen into helium: lower-mass stars mainly by the proton–proton chain ($4\,{}^1_1\text{H} \rightarrow {}^4_2\text{He} + 2\,{}^0_{+1}\text{e} + 2\nu + \gamma$, releasing about 26.7 MeV), and more massive, hotter stars mainly by the CNO cycle, in which carbon acts as a catalyst. When core hydrogen runs out, post-main-sequence stars contract and heat up enough to fuse helium into carbon (triple-alpha process) and, in massive stars, successively heavier elements up to iron. Fusion stops at iron because it has the highest binding energy per nucleon — fusing beyond iron would absorb rather than release energy. The released energy provides the heat and light (luminosity) of stars and the pressure that balances gravity.

questions.question:
The energy levels of helium are shown below ($n = 5$: −2.8 eV; $n = 4$: −3.4 eV; $n = 3$: −6.1 eV; $n = 2$: −13.6 eV; $n = 1$: −54.4 eV).

Calculate the wavelength of light produced by the transition of an electron from level 5 to level 2.
questions.answer:
$$\Delta E = E_5 - E_2 = -2.8 - (-13.6) = 10.8\ \text{eV} = 10.8 \times 1.602 \times 10^{-19} = 1.7302 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{J}$$
$$E = hf = \frac{hc}{\lambda} \Rightarrow \lambda = \frac{hc}{E} = \frac{6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.00 \times 10^{8}}{1.7302 \times 10^{-18}} = 1.15 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}\ (\approx 115\ \text{nm}).$$
(The Rydberg equation applies only to hydrogen, so it cannot be used here.)

questions.question:
Experiments and observations are used to provide evidence for different models of light. The diagrams below show two experiments that support the wave model of light: Diagram A — a double-slit experiment with monochromatic light producing bright and dark bands on a screen; Diagram B — a polarisation experiment in which light passes through a polarising filter and is then blocked by a second filter at 90° to the first.

Explain how these experiments support the wave model of light.
questions.answer:
**Diagram A (double slit).** Light passing through each narrow slit diffracts (spreads out), so the two slits act as coherent sources (Huygens' wavelets). Where the waves from the two slits meet in phase (path difference $m\lambda$) they interfere constructively, giving bright bands; where they meet out of phase (path difference $(m + \tfrac{1}{2})\lambda$) they interfere destructively, giving dark bands. Diffraction and interference are properties only of waves — Newton's particle (corpuscular) model predicts just two bright bands behind the slits — so Young's evenly spaced fringes support the wave model.

**Diagram B (polarisation).** Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave whose electric field oscillates perpendicular to the direction of travel. Unpolarised light has oscillations in all planes; the first polariser transmits only the component oscillating in one plane, giving plane-polarised light of half the intensity. A second polariser at 90° blocks this light completely, and at other angles the transmitted intensity follows Malus' law, $I = I_{\max}\cos^2\theta$. Only a transverse wave has an orientation that can be selected or blocked in this way, so polarisation supports light being a transverse wave.

questions.question:
The solid line on the graph below shows how the intensity of radiation from a black body varies with wavelength at a particular temperature (observed). The dashed line shows the classical physics prediction, which rises without limit at short wavelengths.

Use this example to explain how a new scientific model is developed.
questions.answer:
A new scientific model is developed when observations are made that the current model cannot explain, and a new model is proposed that explains all of the known observations.

- **Observations not supported by the current model:** classical (wave) physics predicted that the intensity of black body radiation would increase without limit as wavelength decreased (the "ultraviolet catastrophe", dashed line). The observed curve instead peaks and falls to zero at short wavelengths, so the classical model failed.
- **New model proposed:** Planck proposed that the energy of the oscillators emitting the radiation is quantised, coming only in discrete packets $E = hf$. This made high-frequency (short-wavelength) emission less likely, and his equation fitted the observed curve exactly.
- **Testing and acceptance:** the quantum idea was then tested and extended by further experiments — e.g. Einstein used light quanta (photons) to explain the photoelectric effect — and as the evidence supported it, the quantum model of light was accepted, replacing the purely classical model for these phenomena.

questions.question:
The wavelengths of the Lyman series of light emitted from a hydrogen atom are shown in the table below.

| Transition $n_i \rightarrow n_f$ | $\dfrac{1}{n_f^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_i^2}$ | Wavelength (nm) | 1/Wavelength ($\times 10^{6}$ m$^{-1}$) |
|---|---|---|---|
| $2 \rightarrow 1$ | 0.75 | 122 | 8.2 |
| $3 \rightarrow 1$ | 0.88 | 103 | 9.7 |
| $4 \rightarrow 1$ | 0.93 | 97 | 10.3 |
| $5 \rightarrow 1$ | 0.96 | 95 | 10.5 |
| $6 \rightarrow 1$ | 0.97 | 94 | 10.7 |

Construct a graph using appropriate data from the table, with $\dfrac{1}{n_f^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_i^2}$ on the horizontal axis (from 0.7 to 1.0), and thus determine an experimental value for Rydberg's constant.
questions.answer:
Plot $\dfrac{1}{\lambda}$ ($\times 10^6$ m$^{-1}$, vertical axis, from about 8 to 11) against $\dfrac{1}{n_f^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_i^2}$ (horizontal axis) and draw a line of best fit through the five points.

The Rydberg equation is
$$\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{n_f^2} - \frac{1}{n_i^2}\right),$$
so this graph is a straight line through the origin with **gradient equal to $R$**.

Using two points on the line of best fit, e.g. $(0.77,\ 8.41 \times 10^6)$ and $(0.95,\ 10.4 \times 10^6)$:
$$R = \text{gradient} = \frac{(10.4 - 8.41) \times 10^{6}}{0.95 - 0.77} = \frac{1.99 \times 10^{6}}{0.18} \approx 1.1 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}.$$
(The accepted value is $1.097 \times 10^{7}$ m$^{-1}$.)

questions.question:
Early experiments determined that cathode rays were beams of small, negatively charged particles, later known as electrons. One of these experiments was the paddlewheel experiment, shown below, in which cathode rays strike a light paddle wheel mounted on rails between the cathode and anode.

Other experiments that confirmed different properties of electrons, like mass and charge, include those done by Millikan and Thomson.

Explain how the paddlewheel experiment and EITHER the Millikan OR Thomson experiment confirmed properties of the electron. You must include a diagram and a quantitative explanation as part of your response.
questions.answer:
**Paddlewheel experiment.** When the cathode rays struck the vanes of the light paddle wheel, the wheel rotated and rolled along its rails away from the cathode. The wheel gained momentum (from zero), so by conservation of momentum the cathode rays must have carried and transferred momentum, $p = mv$. This showed that cathode rays have **mass** — they behave as a stream of particles rather than as waves of light — supporting the particle nature of cathode rays.

**Thomson's experiment (charge-to-mass ratio).** *Diagram:* a cathode ray tube in which the beam passes between two parallel charged plates (electric field $E$, vertical) and through a region of magnetic field $B$ (from coils) perpendicular to both the beam and $E$, striking a fluorescent screen.
1. Both fields were applied and adjusted until the beam was undeflected. The electric and magnetic forces were then balanced:
$$qE = qvB \Rightarrow v = \frac{E}{B}.$$
2. The electric field was switched off, so the magnetic force alone made the beam travel in a circular arc of radius $r$, measured from its deflection:
$$qvB = \frac{mv^2}{r} \Rightarrow \frac{q}{m} = \frac{v}{Br} = \frac{E}{B^2 r}.$$
3. The beam was deflected towards the positive plate, showing negative charge, and $q/m$ was about $1.76 \times 10^{11}$ C kg$^{-1}$ — about 1800 times larger than for a hydrogen ion — and the same whatever cathode metal or gas was used.

This confirmed that cathode rays are negatively charged particles with a very small mass compared with atoms and that they are a common constituent of all matter (the electron).

*(Alternatively, Millikan's oil-drop experiment: charged oil drops between horizontal plates were held stationary by adjusting the voltage, so $qE = mg$, i.e. $q = \dfrac{mgd}{V}$, with $m$ found from the terminal velocity. All charges measured were whole-number multiples of $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C, showing that charge is carried in discrete units — the charge of one electron.)*

questions.question:
A DC motor was turned on. After some time it reached its maximum rotational speed of 100 RPM (revolutions per minute). During this time, the RPM and torque were measured at various points and plotted on the graph below: the torque decreases linearly from 1.6 N m at 0 RPM to 0 N m at 100 RPM.

Explain, with reference to data in the graph, why the torque decreases as the rotational speed of the DC motor increases.
questions.answer:
- The motor produces torque because the current-carrying coil is in a magnetic field: $\tau = nIAB\sin\theta$. With $n$, $A$ and $B$ constant, torque is proportional to the current $I$.
- As the coil rotates, the magnetic flux through it changes, so by Faraday's law an emf is induced in the coil, $\varepsilon = -N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$. By Lenz's law this **back emf** opposes the supply emf that drives the motor.
- The faster the coil rotates, the faster the flux changes (same change in flux in less time), so the back emf is proportional to the rotational speed.
- The net emf is $\varepsilon_{\text{net}} = \varepsilon_{\text{supply}} - \varepsilon_{\text{back}}$, which decreases as speed increases; the current $I = \dfrac{\varepsilon_{\text{net}}}{R}$ decreases, so the torque decreases.
- This matches the graph: at 0 RPM there is no back emf and the torque is maximum (1.6 N m); the torque decreases linearly with RPM, because back emf is proportional to speed; at 100 RPM the torque is zero, meaning the back emf equals the supply emf, so the net emf and current are zero. The motor stops accelerating at this maximum speed (an ideal motor with no friction or load).

questions.question:
A ball is hit at a speed of 35 m s$^{-1}$ from ground level inside a stadium with a roof that is 40 m above the ground.

At the top of the flight of the ball, it just touches the roof and continues on its path, with no impact upon its trajectory. The projectile lands at the same level from which it was launched.

Determine the angle at which the ball must be hit so that it just touches the roof, and thus calculate the range of the ball when it lands. (Ignore air resistance; take $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.)
questions.answer:
**Angle.** At maximum height $v_y = 0$ and $s_y = 40$ m, with $u_y = 35\sin\theta$ and $a_y = -9.8$ m s$^{-2}$:
$$v_y^2 = u_y^2 + 2a_y s_y \Rightarrow 0 = (35\sin\theta)^2 - 2 \times 9.8 \times 40$$
$$(35\sin\theta)^2 = 784 \Rightarrow \sin^2\theta = \frac{784}{35^2} = 0.64 \Rightarrow \sin\theta = 0.8 \Rightarrow \theta = 53.1^\circ.$$

**Time of flight.** $u_y = 35\sin 53.13^\circ = 28$ m s$^{-1}$. Landing at the launch height, $v_y = -28$ m s$^{-1}$:
$$v_y = u_y + a_y t \Rightarrow -28 = 28 - 9.8t \Rightarrow t = 5.714\ \text{s}.$$

**Range.** $u_x = 35\cos 53.13^\circ = 21$ m s$^{-1}$:
$$s_x = u_x t = 21 \times 5.714 \approx 120\ \text{m}.$$

questions.question:
A student made the following claim about the structure of the hydrogen-1 isotope.

> "The atom is made of two fundamental particles. The atom has one electron, bound to the nucleus through the weak nuclear force. The atom has one proton, comprised of three quarks (udd), held together by the strong nuclear force."

Assess the student's claim.
questions.answer:
**Correct parts of the claim:**
- The atom has one electron: correct — a neutral hydrogen-1 atom has a single electron.
- The atom has one proton: correct — all hydrogen isotopes have atomic number 1, and hydrogen-1 has no neutrons.
- The proton is made of three quarks: correct — it is a baryon.
- The quarks are held together by the strong nuclear force: correct — the strong force, mediated by gluons, binds quarks into protons and neutrons.

**Incorrect parts of the claim:**
- "Made of two fundamental particles": incorrect — the electron is a lepton and is fundamental, but the proton is composite (made of quarks), so it is not fundamental. The fundamental particles are the electron and three quarks.
- "Electron bound by the weak nuclear force": incorrect — the electron is bound to the nucleus by the electromagnetic force (attraction between the positive proton and negative electron).
- "Quarks udd": incorrect — a proton is uud, with charge $+\tfrac{2}{3} + \tfrac{2}{3} - \tfrac{1}{3} = +1$; udd has charge 0 and is a neutron.

**Judgement:** although the student correctly identifies the numbers of electrons, protons and quarks and the role of the strong force, the claim is mostly incorrect, because it misidentifies which particles are fundamental, the force binding the electron and the quark composition of the proton.
